{{Short description|Philosophical concept of a most basic substance, or supreme being}}
{{For|other senses of "monad"|Monad (disambiguation){{!}}Monad}}
[[File:Monad.svg|thumb|The circled dot was used by the Pythagoreans and later Greeks to represent the first metaphysical being, the ''Monad'' or the [[Absolute (philosophy)|Absolute]].]]

The term '''''monad''''' ({{ety|grc|''{{lang|grc|μονάς}}'' ({{transliteration|grc|monas}})|unity||''{{lang|grc|μόνος}}'' ({{transliteration|grc|monos}})|alone}})<ref>{{cite web |title=Oxford English Dictionary |url=https://www.oed.com/view/Entry/121054?redirectedFrom=monad#eid |website=www.oed.com |publisher=Oxford University Press |access-date=17 August 2022 |language=en}}</ref> is used in some [[Philosophy of cosmos|cosmic philosophy]] and [[cosmogony]] to refer to a most basic or original substance. As originally conceived by the [[Pythagoreans]], the Monad is, therefore, the Supreme Being, [[divinity]], or the totality of all things. 

According to some philosophers of the [[early modern period]], most notably [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]], there are infinite monads, which are the basic and immense forces, [[elementary particle]]s, or [[Atomism|simplest units]] that make up the universe.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Leibniz |first1=Gottfried Wilhelm, Freiherr von |title=Discourse on metaphysics, and the monadology |date=2005 |publisher=Dover Publications |location=Mineola, N.Y. |isbn=978-0486443102}}</ref>

==Historical background==

=== Ancient Greece ===
According to [[Hippolytus of Rome]], the [[Pythagoreanism|Pythagoreans]] called the first thing that came into existence the "monad", which begat (bore) the [[dyad (philosophy)|dyad]] (from the Greek word for two), which begat the [[number]]s, which begat the [[Point (geometry)|point]], begetting [[line (geometry)|line]]s (or finiteness), and so on.<ref name="diogenes">[[Diogenes Laërtius]], ''[[Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers]]''.</ref> [[Diogenes Laërtius]] similarly held that from the monad evolved the dyad; from it numbers; from numbers, points; then lines, two-dimensional [[entity|entities]], three-dimensional entities, bodies, culminating in the four [[classical element]]s of earth, water, fire and air, from which the rest of our world is built up.<ref name="diogenes" />{{efn|This Pythagorean cosmogony is in some sense similar to a brief passage found in the [[Daoist]] {{transliteration|zh|[[Daodejing|Laozi]]}}: "From the Dao comes one, from one comes two, from two comes three, and from three comes the [[ten thousand things]]".<ref>（道生一、一生二、二生三、三生萬物。）''Dao De Jing'', Chapter 42</ref>}}

For the Pythagoreans, the generation of number series bridged the gap between objects of [[geometry]] and [[cosmogony]] (creation theories).<ref>Sandywell, p. 205. "The generation of the series of number is to the Pythagoreans, in other words, both the generation of the objects of geometry and also cosmogony. Since things equal numbers, the first unit, in generating the number series, is generating also the physical universe. (KR: 256) From this perspective 'the monad' or 'One' was readily identified with the [[divine]] origin of reality."</ref> They thus held the monad as a symbol of [[divinity]], the first being, or the totality of all beings, referring in cosmogony variously to source acting alone or an indivisible origin and [[abstraction (philosophy)|equivalent comparators]].<ref>Fairbanks, Arthur, Ed., "The First Philosophers of Greece". K. Paul, Trench, Trubner. London, 1898, p. 145.</ref>

In the [[Neoplatonic]] metaphysics of [[Proclus]], reality is organized in a fractal-like structure, where the role of the monad is to bind together each layer with the next, such that a monad at a higher level folds out into a multiplicity at a lower level; this lower multiplicity is itself a multiplicity of monads at the next level down.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Perl |first=Eric |date=2020 |title=Proclus’ Multi-Level Ontology: The Meaning of Monads vs. A Tale Told by Thomists |url=https://ojs.library.dal.ca/dionysius/article/view/10772/9535 |format=PDF |journal=[[Dionysius (journal)|Dionysius]] |volume=38 |pages=143–167}}</ref>{{sfn|Chlup|2012|p=103}} Proclus thus writes in the ''[[Elements of Theology]]'' (21.1–3): "Every order of reality has its beginning in a monad and proceeds to a multiplicity coordinate with that monad; and the multiplicity in any order may be referred back to a single monad."{{sfn|Chlup|2012|pp=101–102}}

Some Neoplatonic philosophers, such as [[Plotinus]] and [[Porphyry (philosopher)|Porphyry]], were [[Gnosticism and Neoplatonism#Neoplatonist objections|opposed to Gnosticism]], which they considered broadly synonymous with Christianity as a whole.{{sfn|Butler|2016|p=143}} In ''Against the Gnostics'' (''[[Enneads|Enn.]]'' II.9), Plotinus contends that they "contract the divine into one",{{sfn|Butler|2016|p=150}} thereby accusing them of misapplying Platonic theory about the monad in defense of [[monotheism]].{{sfn|Butler|2016|pp=148–150}}

The idea of the monad is also reflected in the [[demiurge]], or the belief of one supreme being that brought about the [[creation myth|creation of the universe]].{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}}

=== Medieval Christianity ===
In his [[Latin]]-language treaty {{lang|la|Maximae theologiae}}, [[Alain de Lille]] affirms that "God is an intelligible [[sphere]], whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere." The French philosopher [[François Rabelais]] ascribed this proposition to [[Hermes Trismegistus]].<ref name="Gilson-1955">{{cite book |first1=Etienne|last1=Gilson|authorlink= Etienne Gilson|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wlWMDwAAQBAJ6pg|title=History of Christian Philosophy in the Middle Ages|chapter=From Scotus Eriugena to Saint Bernard|isbn=9780813231952|publisher=Catholic University of America Press|location=Washington DC|date=February 15, 2019|oclc=1080547285|pages=173–174, 809}}</ref> This [[Euclid]]ean{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}} [[symbol]]ism of the centered sphere also concerns the [[secular]] debate on the existence of a [[Axis mundi|center of the universe]]. The symbolism is a free [[exegesis]] related to the [[Trinity]] in [[Christian theology]] and influenced by Plotinus.<ref name="Gilson-1955" /> Alain also mentions the ''[[Book of the 24 Philosophers|Book of the Twenty-Four Philosophers]]'', attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, wherein it is stated that a Monad will beget only another Monad;<ref name="Gilson-1955" /> some Christians saw in this the generation, or creation, of [[God the Son]] from [[God the Father]]. This view might be similar to that of the [[pagan]] author of the ''[[Asclepius (treatise)|Asclepius]],''<ref name="Gilson-1955" /> who sometimes has also been identified with Hermes Trismegistus. The ''Book of the Twenty-Four Philosophers'' completes the scheme adding that the ardor of the second Monad to the first Monad would be the [[Holy Spirit in Christianity]].<ref name="Gilson-1955" /> It closes a physical circle in a logical triangle (with a [[retraction (topology)|retroaction]]).

==Modern philosophy==
The term monad was adopted from [[Greek philosophy]] by a number of [[Modern philosophy|modern philosophers]], including [[Giordano Bruno]], [[Anne Conway (philosopher)|Anne Conway]], [[John Dee]] (''[[Monas Hieroglyphica|The Hieroglyphic Monad]]''), and [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]] (''[[Monadology]]''). The concept of the monad as a universal substance is also used by [[Theosophy|Theosophists]] as a synonym for the [[Sanskrit]] term "[[svabhava]]t"; [[The Mahatma Letters to A.P. Sinnett|the Mahatma Letters]] make frequent use of the term.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Barker |first=A. Trevor |title=The Mahatma Letters to A.P. Sinnett |isbn=1-55700-086-7}}</ref>
